newsitem.title: USA: Japan trade surplus still concerns U.S. -- Summers.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus still concerns U.S. -- Summers.

text.p: Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Wednesday the United States remained concerned about a rise in the Japanese trade surplus.

"We have been expressing concerns for some time about Japan and about the dangerous possibility that the Japanese current account surplus would expand substantially," Summers told the Charlie Rose television talk show in New York.

Summers said Japan's current account suplus could expand if Japan did not take necessary steps, particularly through fiscal policy, to ensure adequate growth there led by Japanese domestic demand, Summers said.
It was also vital to have adequate growth in Europe, Summers said, because a growing and prosperous Europe would be a better trading partner for the United States.

"We have to be very concerned that Europe take the steps that are necessary to create the kind of flexibilities that would enable their economy to grow and that, as they move forward with the monetary union project, they remember ultimately its success and their economic success depends upon their attainment of a reasonable rate of growth," he said.
More rapid growth in both Japan and Europe would spur faster growth in demand for U.S. exports, in turn reducing the trade balance, Summers said.
"A lower trade balance surely would increase the overall health of the economy," he said. "I think it's important we see more growth in Europe and in Japan."

When asked about the U.S. economic outlook, especially in view of yesterday's Federal Reserve quarter-percentage point short-term rate increase, Summers said the U.S. economy was robust while showing no real signs of increased inflation.

"The energy of what the private sector has done in recent years, the progress we've made in bringing down the budget deficit, creates a situation where we've got something we haven't had in a long time -- an investment-led, low-inflation recovery with strong export performance," he said.
Summers, when asked to predict where the U.S. economy would be by the end of 1997, said the growth rate should remain steady, fluctuating quarter to quarter between two and three percent.
"One has to be tremendously encouraged by the fact that the economy could be this strong, with this much demand pressure, without any real evidence of increasing inflation," Summers said.
He said: "I don't make prescriptions for the Federal Reserve, but this is a very robust economy."

An economic structural shift towards more flexibility, services and internationalisation, as well as better inventory control, may have also attenuated the volatility of the business cycle, Summers said. -- New York newsdesk 212-859-1610
